reference.source: Textbook of Pediatric Rheumatology / ILAR & PRINTO criteria
clinicalPearls: Localised scleroderma is confined to the skin and underlying tissues and, unlike systemic sclerosis, does not cause Raynaud phenomenon or internal organ fibrosis
The linear subtype is the commonest form in children and can extend through subcutaneous fat, muscle and bone, impairing growth of the affected limb
The en coup de sabre variant is a linear lesion on the scalp or face that can be associated with underlying neurological and ophthalmological problems and hemifacial atrophy
Active lesions show an erythematous or violaceous advancing border, while established plaques become sclerotic, waxy and hypo- or hyperpigmented
Linear lesions crossing joints may cause contractures and limb-length discrepancy, so functional and growth monitoring is important
Extracutaneous features such as arthritis, seizures and uveitis can accompany more extensive disease
Methotrexate, often with a course of systemic corticosteroids, is used for active, extending or functionally threatening disease
reference.pathophysiology: Juvenile localised scleroderma is an immune-mediated fibrosing disorder of the skin and deeper tissues. Early inflammation with lymphocytic infiltration and endothelial activation is followed by fibroblast activation and excessive deposition of collagen and extracellular matrix, producing progressive sclerosis. In linear and en coup de sabre forms the fibrotic process can extend into fascia, muscle, bone and, on the face, adjacent structures, so that involvement over a growing limb or the developing face leads to atrophy, contracture and growth disturbance rather than the internal organ fibrosis seen in systemic sclerosis.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical scoring of lesion activity and skin thickness for monitoring
Antinuclear antibody, which may be positive but is non-specific
MRI of affected limb or face to assess depth of involvement and central nervous system changes in en coup de sabre
Ophthalmology assessment for uveitis in craniofacial disease
Skin biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain
Limb-length and joint range assessment for functional monitoring
Thermography or ultrasound to help gauge disease activity where available
redFlags: Rapidly extending linear lesions crossing joints threatening contracture
Craniofacial (en coup de sabre) disease with seizures, headache or focal neurological signs
Progressive limb-length discrepancy or hemifacial atrophy in a growing child
reference.prognosis: Many lesions eventually become inactive, but linear and deep disease can leave permanent cosmetic and functional deficits, including limb-length discrepancy, contractures and facial atrophy. Early immunosuppression during the active phase improves outcomes and reduces long-term morbidity.
pitfalls: Mistaking early inflammatory lesions for eczema or infection and delaying treatment
Assuming localised disease will always remain purely cutaneous and missing deep or neurological extension
Failing to monitor growth and joint function in linear disease
Overlooking ophthalmological and neurological screening in en coup de sabre
Treating only established fibrosis, when therapy is most effective during active inflammation
references: PRINTO/PReS recommendations for juvenile localised scleroderma
Consensus guidance on paediatric morphoea management
